Thefollowing typesof software areusedinteaching mathematics: • software of general purpose; • professional software for mathematicians and engineers: ◦ Computer Algebra Systems (CAS); ◦ Interactive Geometry Software (IGS)/Dynamic Geometry Environments (DGEs); • software designed specifically for teaching mathematics. Software of general purpose (PowerPoint, Excel, etc.) is often publicly available and familiar to most students. It can be applied in the study of mathematics, although in the vast majority of cases, it does not supportin-depth learning of the subject. On the other hand, the lack of mathematical orientation of this type of software allows to focus students’ attention on typical mistakes and ideas for their correction (see model M2.9 in Chapter 2). Big packages, for example, Microsoft Office, often include support for the possibility of their expansion and adaptation, thanks to the presence of built-in programming tools likeVisualBasicforApplications (VBA).With their help, onecandevelopeasilyandquicklyspecializedprogrammodules for studying concrete mathematical subjects (see Sections 1.1.5 and 1.1.6 in Chapter 1).

Mathematics is a unified science, and one of the pedagogical goals is to emphasize, to demonstrate this fact to students. Educational software can play an important role here. It is important to seek a unified software, withaunifiedinterface, whichisusedwhenstudying a wide variety of subjects: algebra, geometry, calculus, etc. The universal validity of mathematical statement theorems and their invariance concerning a variety of objects that satisfy their conditions necessitate appropriate support in computer models. IGS-DGE sufficiently complies with this requirement. The situation is different with models of non-geometric content. Awareness of the importance of the mentioned issues has led the 4 author to develop a new, non-commercial software (VisuMatica), designed as far as possible to solve them. 4As an illustration, let us refer to our with Gabriel Katz book The Shape of Algebra in the Mirrors of Mathematics (Katz and Nodelman, 2012), whose title alone speaks for itself. ThisbookincludesaCD-ROMwithVisuMatica, whichallowsemphasizingthe unity of different areas of mathematics and their“help” to each other.

About the Author Vladimir Nodelman began teaching mathematicsatschoolin1970shortlybeforegraduating from the Belarusian State University (MSc inmathematics).Realizingthepotentialofeducational technology (at that time classical), he began to explore the possibilities of developing and using teaching aids while working on his dissertation in Moscow, at the Academy of Pedagogical Sciences of the USSR (PhD in 1970s). Hepublishedseveralarticles inthefield of didactics of mathematics and pedagogical psychology and developed various mathematics teaching aids, including electronic devices that are widely replicated and used in USSR schools. While teaching higher mathematics and methods of mathematics at the university, he patented several devices for modeling the fundamental concepts of Calculus. In the early 1980s, it was planned to switch to the study of computer science and the introduction of computers in schools. The author of this book was invited to the experimental laboratory of one of the closed institutions in Moscow, where hewas shown a computer program simulating the operation of one of his devices. It was an amazing surprise that led him to realize that most mathematical models, which are dynamic constructs with meaningful information on a front flat panel, can be presented on a computer screen. At the time of the formation of the Laboratory of Informatics at the Belarusian Research Institute of Pedagogy, Dr. Nodelman began xiii

xiv Mathematics Studies Through Technology: Precalculus, Calculus, and More working thereas asenior scientist. Along with research in thefield of methods for teaching computer science and the publication of relevant articles, hestarted tofigureouttheprinciplesof theapplication of computers in education, and in particular in teaching mathematics, and creating educational software. Some results of these studies he publishes in the book Computer as an Educational Aids. After repatriating to Israel in 1990, he teaches mathematics and computer science and continues to develop mathematics educational software for which he received an international award. An analysis of experience in the creation and use of software for teaching mathematics led him to the conclusion that such software should be a single program instead of distinct programs on different topics and areas of mathematics. From that moment (the mid-1990s), he began and went on to this day the development of the VisuMatica program. This software allows one to explore interactively and VISUally matheMATICAl content. This book makes extensive use of VisuMatica. For over 30 years, the author has been a faculty member of the Department of Computer Science of the School of Computer Science at the Holon Institute of Technology. The main area of his scientific research remains unchanged — the ways of teaching mathematics using educational software. The results of these studies and many of the book’s ideas were publishedin articles and reported at numerous international conferences.

# Chapter 1

Counterexamples in Mathematics Education: Why, Where, and How? A counterexample is an example that disproves the trueness of some statement. For a mathematician, constructing a counterexample is a common way to refute mathematical conjectures. Counterexamples also help here to establish the constraints imposed on theorems. In mathematics education, counterexamples can and should be applied at the earliest stages — in the study of concepts, long before the first acquaintance with the theorems and proofs. Herewith, the use of software becomes an organic element of the learning process. 1 Studies of Concepts In the definition of any concept, one can distinguish between two components: substantive and logical. With that, the content component is always specific, while the logical one very often coincides. For example, thefollowing two definitionsdefinecompletely different concepts, buttheir logical structureis thesame: this is aconjunction of two features: A parallelogram is a quadrangle with opposite sides parallel: parallelogram ⇔ (1) quadrangle ∧ (2) opposite sides parallel. An equation is an equality containing a variable: ⇔ ∧ equation (1) equality (2) contains a variable. 1

2 Mathematics Studies Through Technology: Precalculus, Calculus, and More The commonality of logical structures allows us to build a general approach to the formation of concepts in teaching mathematics. 1.1 Propositional definitions We consider here the place and role of counterexamples in the teaching of concepts with the frequent logical structures of the propositional definition. 1.1.1 The principle of variation of non-essential features From the very early moments of their life, children meet mathematical objects and acquire skills of their recognition. Pedagogical psychology provides the principle of variation of non-essential features (Menchinskaya, 1971) (while the essential features are kept invariable). It is intended to illustrate essential features of a concept by demonstrating various visual materials and examples or to highlight essential characteristics of a concept by varying non-essential features. The goal of using variation is to help students understand the essential features ofaconceptbydifferentiating themfromnonessential ones and, further, by the assimilation of a scientific concept (Rongjin and Yeping, 2017). The common, which in this approach is identified with the essential, repeatedly acting on the person, each time reinforces the reflection of this common. Non-essential, on the contrary, is presented every time with a new concrete form, is erased and does not enter into the content of the concept. In this case, non-essential features should not only vary but also be contrasted with essential ones. That is, simultaneously with the consideration of objects in which non-essential characteristics vary, the teacher must emphasize that the essential characteristics remain unchanged. A widespread example of the use of this principle in mathematics teachers’ literature is the recommendation to illustrate the notion of the right triangle by drawing it in a different orientation, not exclusivelywithverticalandhorizontalcatheti. Onecanaddavariety of colors, materials, sizes, etc., if she is “afraid”, that in case of all models in the lesson are made from blue cardboard, students will think that to be a right triangle the figure should (a) be a triangle,

Counterexamples in Mathematics Education 3 (b) have a right angle, (c) have a blue color, and (d) made from cardboard. In this situation, the teacher faces a problem: which of the non-essential attributes should be varied, and which could be omitted? In fact, unlike the finite number of essential features, there are “infinitely” many non-essential ones. Needless to say, the same situation exists in the development of software intended to facilitate the formation and assimilation of concepts:...It is impossible to implement such an unconstructive pedagogical approach. This principle has been convincingly criticized in the psychological literature (Talyzina, 1995). Without denying its role in situations of uncontrolledorpoorlymanagedassimilation ofconcepts, itexpresses the associative approach to understandthe process of assimilation of concepts. 1.1.2 An active recognition of belonging to the concept We will treat the principle of variation of non-essential features as a minor way of learning and consider instead an active recognition, based on the definition of a mathematical concept. Each definition consists of contextual and logical constituents. The majority of concepts studied in elementary, secondary, and high school have a conjunctive definition with two or three attributes. There are 2 n combinations of values in the corresponding truth n table, which describes the logic of a definition with attributes. Clearly, it will be sufficient to consider only these cases in the concept’s studies. Each case presents a type of task: objects with a definite combination of truth values of the essential-only features. Any conceivable recognition object necessarily represents only one of these types.

Theproposedmethodsforthestudyofconceptsformanddevelop the necessary skills, often long before the students’ first encounters with theorems and their proofs thereby removing the stress of novelty, and facilitating understanding. 1.1.7 Effectiveness The experimental verification of the proposed way of studying concepts was carried out with 10–11-year-old students of two primary school classes for a period of half a year. During the experiment, it was detected that the students found it possible to separate the logic of definitions from the specific content of their features. They increasingly used the expressions “first feature”, and “second feature” instead of “sides are equal”, “right angle”, etc. For this reason, the final test included the tasks for completing the truth tables, such as the following one: “starting from theunknown(ortheconclusion) andworkingbackwards”(Polya, 2004, p.200).

Counterexamples in Mathematics Education 15 Has the first feature Has Has AND the first featurethe second featurehas the second feature False False False True True False True True Testing the skills of the logical action of concluding was carried outontaskswithtrivialcontent(nomathematics)toexcludepossible mistakes of misunderstanding the subject of the task, for example: The box contains wooden and plastic balls of different colors. All the wooden balls are red. — Ana took a wooden ball out of the box. Is this ball red? — Mike took a red ball out of the box. Is this a wooden ball? — Tom took a plastic ball out of the box. Is this a red ball? — Dan took a blue ball out of the box. Is this a wooden ball? The grades on the test were surprisingly high. This prompted us to offer this test to other groups and compare the results. It turned out thatthestudents’gradesintheexperimentalclasseswerestatistically higher not only in comparison with their peers not participating in the experiment but even in comparison with the results of the high school graduates. These facts demonstrate the fundamental role of the mental actions of recognition, and of concluding from the fact of belonging or not belonging to the concept in the process of mastering the concept as well as in the development of students’ logical thinking, in the formation of the abilities and needs in proof. Experimental results show the effectiveness of the proposed approach, supported by technological aids. 1.2 Predicate logic Most concepts in calculus have a definition that includes quantifiers. The logical structure of these definitions is different almost in every specific case. Our approach to constructing the task types, which we discovered for propositional definitions in the previous section, is

Moreover, any subcurve defined on the interval [0,a], where 0 < a ≤ 1 also has an infinite length. Space-filling curves provide much more interesting examples of curves with an infinite length. Consider the Hilbert curve, a well-known example of such a curve.

24 Mathematics Studies Through Technology: Precalculus, Calculus, and More Hilbert’s principle is as follows. If the interval I can be continuously mapped to a square Q, then after dividing I into four congruent subintervals and Q into four congruent subsquares, each subinterval can be mapped continuously to one of the subsquares. Then each subinterval, in turn, is divided into four congruent subintervals, and each subsquare into four congruent subsquares, and so 2n on. If this goes on indefinitely, then Q and I break up into 2 congruent copies for n = 1,2,3. Hilbert showed that it is possible to arrange subsquares so that the adjacent subintervals would correspond to adjacent subsquares with the common side and so that the inclusion relation is preserved, i.e., if the square corresponds to an interval, then its subsquares correspond to the subintervals of this interval (Sagan, 1994; Bader, 2017). Model M1.6 (see the file Hilbert colored MAPPING.grh) implements this construction. Figure 16 displays the cited process for the starting steps (1, 2, 3, 5, and 10). The spectrum-rainbow-colored horizontal segment models interval I and the unit square–square Q. The subdivision squares are presented by the gridlines. Color code expresses the mapping correspondence: the point with coordinate c on the interval I and its image, point (x,y), in Q have the same color. Considering step curves (polygonal chains) as approximations of the Hilbert curve, 13 one can see that their length — length 14 (Hilbert) — grows very quickly. However, it remains unclear whether the growth is limited and if the Hilbert curve has an infinite length. Ontheotherhand, itisclear thattheHilbertcurvefillsthewhole Q. It looks as if even the “curve” in step 10 (Fig. 16(e)) completely fills out the square. Nevertheless, every rectifiable curve is a zero set, i.e., it can be enclosed in a polygonal figure of an arbitrarily small F, area. It is worth noting an interesting connection between the authors of the mentioned counterexamples. Here, one cannot do without another outstanding mathematician: Giuseppe Peano. It was he who discovered the first example of a space-filling curve (1890). David Hilbertproposedhiscurvein1891 asavariantofthePeanocurve.In 1882, Peano independently from Schwarz also discovered the CylinderAreaParadox.ItwashisfirstresultinCalculus.WhenPeanotold his teacher Angelo Genocci, he informed him that already in 1880, he received a letter from Hermann Schwarz describingthis discovery. Schwartz officially published his counterexample only in 1890.

# Chapter 2

Functional Line in Mathematics Studies We, who are called the reformers, would put the function conceptattheverycenterofinstruction, because, ofalltheconcepts of the mathematics of the past two centuries, this one plays the leading role wherever mathematical thought is used. We would introduce it into instruction as early as possible with constant use of the graphical method, the representation of functional x y relations in the system, which is used today as a matter of course in every practical application of mathematics. —Klein, 2004, p. 4 1 Fundamental Notions The two fundamental concepts of the functional line — variable and function — and different approaches to their studies have been discussed for a long time in the didactics of mathematics (Freudenthal, 2002; Eisenberg, 2002), etc.:
• A variable has a name and a value, which is an element of a set of
any nature.
• A function is a relation between elements of some set(s).
As a means of modeling and organizing of assimilation of these concepts, especially at the initial stages, one can use Microsoft Excel. The software has the following advantages: • It is publicly available. • Students already in middle school know how to use it. 43

44 Mathematics Studies Through Technology: Precalculus, Calculus, and More
• Its internal mechanism of information presentation is initially ade-
quate to the notion of variable. Every cell in Excel has a name and avalue. Bydefault, thenameisanaddress, forexample,“C3”,but thecellcanbe“renamed”tosomethingmoremeaningful, e.g.,“x”. The value in the cell’s contents is the information of any nature: numerical, textual, and graphical. • Thebuilt-inmechanismofinformationprocessinginExcelassumes an explicit definition of relations between cells by the user. • The user interface of Excel allows the construction of simple but proper educational models without any sort of programming. 1.1 Propaedeutic stage The theme of Expressions provides a convenient platform to organize an implicit familiarity of middle school students with notions of variable and function using a chain of simple activities that starts from an empty worksheet and fluently transforms into an intensive 1 use of the scrollbar control (Nodelman, 1997). We start from a simple “machine” of two cells A1 and A2 — model M2.1 (see Tab PROCESSOR). A1 is an INPUT and we call A2 the PROCESSOR (Fig. 1(a)). The following task implicitly prepares students for the concept of an inverse function: • Define Inverter DO-UNDO — a conveyor with two machines, whose result always equals the input: “2∗x”. (a) The first processor is What is the second one? Check your answer with Excel. (b) Define a few more inverters. (c) Does the expression of the second PROCESSOR uniquely depend on the first one? (d) Will the conveyor work properly after replacing the order of its two machines? (e) Why is this conveyor called an Inverter DO-UNDO? Thequestofinitialnumberxthatresultsinadefinitek is, actually, a k quest of preimage of value of the function presented by expression. In other words, it is a task of solution of equation f(x)= k. Fill in the Goal Seek dialog box and click OK. Voila! You got the necessary INPUT value and all the results of the inner machines in the conveyor (Fig. 6). 52 Mathematics Studies Through Technology: Precalculus, Calculus, and More Now, we have a range of proper examples and counterexamples to introduce the definition of the notion of function and organize its assimilation: activities of recognition and deducing corollaries. The next step in studying this concept is familiarizing with different ways of representing functions: tabular, analytical, graphical, and verbal. The accumulated experience in Excel already gave students anideaof someof them. Alogical continuation ofthisacquaintance should become the ordering and replenishment of knowledge, a comparative analysis of the advantages and shortcomings of different ways of representing functions, and an awareness of the limits of their applicability. Thefollowing modelsshowpossibleways tosolve formulated pedagogical tasks using suitable software: (1) M2.7: The self-explanatory Fig. 9 presents function y = x2/10 graphically (see the f(x) worksheet in Function.xls). We start the demonstration of graphical modeling from this example for a few reasons: (a) to introduce notions of predefined function’s domain and 8 range as subsets of the same axis of real numbers; (b) to pay attention to the limitation of a scaled axis: Initially, the scrollbar “produces” x ∈ [−10,10]. 9 So, the range is [0, 10] and thus both domain (swept by the pink point) and range (swept by the red arrow pike) are “visible”. Figure 9. 8Thelong-familiar termsinput and output andthesystem of tasksthat offered during period of propaedeutic facilitate theunderstanding. 9Thescrollbargeneratesintegersininterval0...2000tothehiddencellB4.The value of B2 is definedas “=(B4−1000)/100”.

Functional Line in Mathematics Studies 53 Studentsdiscovertheproblemofvisibilityafterchanging the domain interval to [−20,20] by a proper redefinition of cell B2: the red arrow escapes from the graph bounds. Nevertheless, the values of cell C2 still help in finding the range. (c) To pay attention to the inconvenience of representing functional relation by a single arrow and to its insufficient visual potential: Initially, the scrollbar “produces” x ∈ [−10,10]. So, the range is [0, 10] and thus both domain (swept by the pink point) and range (swept by the red arrow pike) are “visible”. Moreover, the changes themselves in the position and direction of the arrow are inexpressive and do not facilitate the perception of the functional relation. However, by offering to experiment with this model by changing the analytical definition of the function (the expression in cell C2), we should draw their attention to that in the case of a linear function, the model becomes very expressive visually. (2) M2.8: Unlike previous models, which theteacher, as well as students, can easily create and modify, the modelin Fig. 10 (see the functional relation worksheetinFunction.xls) isasoftwareproduct programmed with VBA and intended solely for use without any changes. Every time the user presses the New! button, the model producesarandom functionwithadomainofintegersintheinterval [1, 20]. The domain is shown in cells of the 5th row. The corresponding function values are presented in the cells of the 6th row directly under proper argument values. Arc-shaped arrows emphasize the relation visually. The model has two regimes: Correspondence and Permutation, and three options of view: table with arrows, graph, and both (Fig. 10). Starting with table with arrows (and hidden graph), students have a comfortable graphical show that helps them to explore the current function: (a) Is the model an example of a function? Why? (b) What is the function value for arguments 3, 7, 10?

54 Mathematics Studies Through Technology: Precalculus, Calculus, and More Figure 10. (c) What is the argument value(s) that lead to values 1, 2, 14, and 10 of the function? (d) What are its domain and range? (e) How many domain numbers have changed their place? (f) What is the meaning of vertical arrow(s)? In the regime of permutation, one discovers the specific features 10 ofpermutations:orbits, fixed points, cycles, transpositions, etc. Ofcourse, theteacherpre-explainsthemeaningoftheseconcepts 10We recall that a permutation σ of a finite set N,|N| = n, is a bijection of N onto itself. The orbit of x∈N for a permutation σ is thesubset of N consisting of the points x, σ(x), σ2(x)...,σk−1(x), where k, the length of the orbit, is the smallest integer ≥1such that σk(x)=x. If k=1, then x is a fixed point of σ. Let x 1, x 2,...,x k be k different points of N,l ≤ k ≤ n. The cycle γ = (x 1,x 2,...,x k) is the following permutation: γ(x 1) = x 2,γ(x 2) = x 3,...,γ(x k−1) = x k,γ(x k) = x 1, and γ(x) = x if x= x i. We say that γ has length k and has theset {x 1,x 2,...,x k } for domain (or orbit). A circular permutation is a cycle of length n(=|N|). Atransposition τ isacycleoflength2:inotherwords, thereexisttwopoints a and b, a=b, such that τ(b)=a.

Functional Line in Mathematics Studies 55 onanintuitivelevel, forexample, byusingamodelofaparticular permutation. Here students “officially” meet the 2D graphical representation ofthestudiedfunctionforthefirsttime. Fromapedagogical point of view is very important the fact that this meeting happens on an example of functions of a finite nature. In this case, thedomainandrangeofthefunctionarecorrectly readablefrom the graph with proper scales of its axes. At this stage, students’ activities should be concentrated on the formation of skills of “reading” graphs. One can organize it by the same set of questions (1)–(5). The only difference is in the 6th question, which can be reformulated as follows: “What is the meaning of a point, located on the diagonal?” or “Where are the fixed points in the graph?” First, tohelp students, theview option can besetto both and afterward switching to graph hides the table with arrows and enforces exploration of the current function exclusively using a graph. A graphical view of permutations guarantees visualization of one-to-one, bijection relations and consideration of their specifics. image of their Range? 1.3 Precalculus: Elementary functions The functional line in Precalculus is presented in two ways: (1) General properties and operations on functions:
• even and odd, monotonic, and periodic functions;
• inverting, composing, and decomposing functions;
• operations on functions: sums, differences, products, and
quotients;
• transformations of functions.
(2) Functions of specific types:
• polynomial and rational functions;
• exponential and logarithmic functions;
• trigonometric functions.
Studies of all subjects of the rest of the course — sequences, limits, conics, equations, inequalities, and their systems — are actively “using and developing” the content and methods, associated with the concept of function. 1.3.1 General properties and operations on functions The task of constructing mathematical models includes important pedagogical aspects. The developer has to grasp clearly the 16 following: (a) What features does he plan to model? (b) What is their mathematical expression? 16Thedevelopingofspecificmodelscanbedonebystudentsandcanturnintoa challenging project.

Functional Line in Mathematics Studies 71 (c) What is their visual expression? (d) What dynamic interface fits these features? (e) What are the ways of the model’s universalization? Consider models that support the introduction and studies of functions with specific properties. The expected learning outcome consists of explicit understanding and skilled active application of the assimilated properties of a function, in exploration and graphing functions in further studies, in particular, in studies of functions of specific types. (1) “Even function” f(x) is characterized by holding the equation f(x) = f(−x) for every x in the domain. So, we have the following: (a) Our model is designed to express the examination of two features:
• The equality f(x)= f(−x) for every x in the domain.
• Simultaneousbelongingofxand−xtothedomainoff(x)
(implicitly contained in the definition). (b) Visual presentation should emphasize the equality by two points:(x,f(x))and(−x,f(−x)),havingthesameapplicate coordinate for each x from the domain. (c) User interface has to allow assigning any value from the domain of function f to the x variable. (d) The model has to work with different functions. M2.19 — Implementation:

Students’ activities with this model are also similar to the previously discussed. As a rule, the teacher provides examples and counterexamples. However, the task of inventing them always attracts students. Consider the following situation in a classroom: The teacher asks students if the statement the only function which isboth even and odd isthe constant function which is identically zero (i.e., f(x) = 0 for all real x) is correct. He slightly hints to refute statements with...the only...enough to come upwith atleast onecounterexample. Ifit doesnothelp, thenext hint is the subject of the domain. Students grasp the idea and proposeto limit the domain by any symmetric interval. OK, it is the disproof! The teacher carries them further. He asks to propose an analytical expression of a function with a discontinuous y 0 domain. (3) Forthemodelfor“monotonicfunctions”(strictly increasing),we base on the following definition: A function f(x) is called strictly increasing if (∀x 1,x 2 ∈ D(f))(x 1 < x 2 ⇒ f(x 1) < f(x 2)), where D(f) is the domain of f(x). Our model is designed to express the examination of the conjunction of features:
• ∀x 1, x 2 ∈ D(f).
• X 1 < x 2.

The correct statements are the following:
• The monotonic function passes the Horizontal Line Test. 19

After studying the issue of functions increasing and decreasing, it is natural to try to figure out if there is a more delicate, quantitative characteristic of these true/false-valued features of a function’s behavior.

Functional Line in Mathematics Studies 83 The concept of rate of change represented by derivative is the answer to our needs. The propaedeutic of this notion in Precalculus courses is implemented in studies of the concept of the average rate 25 of change. Taking into account the importance of the concept of derivative in mathematics and students’ mathematical culture, we must set correct accents in the study of an average rate of change having in mind its future evolution in Calculus. By definition, the average rate of change of function f(x) is the value of the ratio f(b)−f(a) when b= a and both a and b belong to the b−a domain of f(x). The average rate of change has a visual interpretation as a slope of the secant line that passes through (a, f(a)) and (b, f(b)). 26 It is clear what model we are going to build (Fig. 29). (4) Periodic functions: A function f is said to be periodic if there exists a positive number P such that f(x+P)= f(x) for all x in the domain. The least number P for which this occurs is called the period of f. Our model is intended to express the examination of equality f(x+P) = f(x) for all x in the domain, while P has a definite positive value(s). 27 One can consider equality as follows: (a) (1) An equality of two functions y = f(x+P) and y = f(x). (2) All x in the domain. 27In a class, which is already familiar with transformations of functions and proper ways of exploration, the visual interpretation of equality as coincidence of initial and horizontally transformed graph will be very fruitful and can be considered as a replacement of thecase a (1).

In a proper audience, an adequate model can be constructed in 3D by interpreting variable P as y, and graphing functions f(x + P) as surface z = f(x + y), and f(x) as surface z = f(x). Thus, the task of solving equation f(x+P) = f(x) becomes a task of looking for such value of y that f(x+y) = f(x), namely, the two surfaces coincide (= intersect) along a curve with a constant value of y. This value is the sought-for value of P. Fortunately, this kind of work can be arranged with the help of clipping plane y = P (Fig. 34(d)) (see the file Periodic function-3D.grh). # Chapter 3

Functional Line in the Studies of Equations and Inequalities The basic ideas of the functional line can be useful in the formation of an understanding of the concept of equation/inequality as well as the concept of its solution. The graphing method allows constructing adequate visualizations of complex and even formally unsolvable problems, to observe and study their solutions in generalized form. Leaving the domain of the equation in favor of the higher dimensional modeling is essential for the graphing method and provides a common approach to the visualization of solutions that permits the revealing of their origin. 1 Equation
| An equation |  | is an | equality | containing |  | one or more | variables. |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

118 Mathematics Studies Through Technology: Precalculus, Calculus, and More (1) The coincidence of the roots of equation f(x) = 0 and zeroes of the function y = f(x) links the two notions and provides an understanding of the role of function graphs in studies of equations with one variable. (2) Understanding the solution of equation f(x) = a as the set of preimages of the points on the graph of function f(x) with ordinate a, and the case of a = 0 as a particular although very essential occasion, has an important general outlook. We discuss its application in 1.2. (3) Equations f(x) = a represent a large group of typical p√roblems studiedcompulsorilyinmathematics: ex = a,log x = a, x = a, b etc. An important characteristic of an equation is its domain: all the values of x that can be plugged into the equation. The domain of equation f 1(x) = f 2(x) is the intersection of domains’ of functions f 1(x) and f 2(x). Finding the domain of the equation and keeping in mind the selection of proper and discarding “extraneous” roots are an essential component of the process of solution. VisuMatica makes it automatically. But we have to recognize the limitation of the software — it shows only a limited interval [x min,x max] ⊂ R, and thus not the whole domain and solutions are presented in the view. Of course, one can redefine this interval, but it will never be the whole R. The analytic consideration, based on the features of functions f 1(x) and f 2(x), with the help of graphical visualization using VisuMatica, helps grasp the complete solution. Ancient Greeks knew and studied the properties of these curves. They did not know how to represent them algebraically, but they understood their nature. They understood that such curves can be obtained by cutting a cone with a plane located in a certain way. Three types of curves have received special names:
• An ellipse is a closed curve that is formed when a plane cuts a
cone (Fig. 5(a)).
• A cut by a plane that is parallel to exactly one generatrix of the
| cone forms | an unbounded |  | curve | — a | parabola (Fig. | 5(b)). |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
• A hyperbola is formed in the section of a double cone by a plane, which intersects both halves but does not pass through the apex of a cone (Fig. 5(c)). The teacher summarizes this fact by emphasizing the infinite countable and continuum cases. 1.3 Equation with three variables13 It seems that the case of equations in three variables f(x,y,z) = 0 can beexplored by analogy with the approaches presented in 1.1 and 1.2. However, it cannot! Typically, the solution to these equations is a three-dimensional set. Therefore, we would need one more — four-dimensional space to implement the analogy, i.e., to consider some surfacef(x,y,z) = w andobserve the“contour surfaces” while w-coordinate approaching the value of to 0. Unfortunately, one cannot implement nor perceive direct visualizations of this kind. The only dynamic show one can get is the changing solution of the family of equations itself — the “contour surface”, often called isosurface — following the specific value of variable w as a numeric parameter. So, limited possibility can be useful when considering some types of equations. Really, in this case, we mainly deal with imaging and exploration of surfaces, and this is already a subject not only of calculus but also of geometry. At least, here we can provide the opportunity to feel this interdisciplinary connection. 1.3.1 Explicit form z f(x,y), x f(y,z), The equalities, reducible to an explicit form = = and y = f(x,z), represent functions of two independent variables and are examples of equations in three variables. The function graph (generally, a surface) is the graph of the equation. 152 Mathematics Studies Through Technology: Precalculus, Calculus, and More 1.3.2 Implicit form 1.3.2.1 Bivariate case One can consider the bivariate equations f(x,y) = 0, f(y,z) = 0, and f(x,z) = 0 as a special case of equations in three variables f(x,y) = 0∗z, f(y,z) = 0∗x, and f(x,z) = 0∗y. From this point of view, their solutions are surfaces in 3D. We encountered a similar situation when considering equations with one variable (1.1). We graphed their solutions as sets of 2D lines instead of sets of points on an axis. So, what are the surfaces? Yes, they includeplanargraphsof thebivariate equations incoordinateplanesOxy, Oyz, andOxz correspondingly. Moreofthis, they consist of all the 3D points whose x and y (in case of f(x,y) = 0), y and z (in case of f(y,z)= 0), and x and z (in case of f(x,z) = 0) coordinates satisfy the equation. The geometry of these surfaces becomes clear. For each solution point lying in the corresponding coordinate plane, the entire line containing thispointandperpendiculartotheplaneconsists ofthose and only those points whose two corresponding coordinates coincide with the coordinates of the point. All these lines form the required surface — once more a perpendicular straight line: The only difference is the space dimension, but as before, it is perpendicularfromspaceofdimensionn−1tospaceofdimension n (from 1D to 2D, from 2D to 3D). Such surfaces are called cylindrical. They consist of all points of all the straight lines that are parallel to a given one and pass through all the points of a given planar set (curve). Herewith, this straight line does not belong to the plane of the curve. Our surfaces are formed by the perpendicularsto the plane of the curve. We call them right cylindrical surfaces. Functional Line in the Studies of Equations and Inequalities 175 2.3 System of equations and inequalities Visualization of the nature of the solution of systems of equations and inequalities is a demonstration of graphs of each one of their constituents (single equation or inequality) andthesolution as intersection (union, in case of disjunctive systems) of these graphs. VisuMatica supportsthedefinition of systems by separating their constituents by the sign of semicolon (;). The disjunctive system is defined by the sign of the vertical bar (|). Figure 42 presents the way of typing definition in the main input box and its visualization in VisuMatica. It is necessary to draw attention to the different meanings of a curlybracketinthesymbolicnotation ofpiecewisefunctions:itholds the disjunction of conditions, expressed in the lines. The formal interpretation of square brackets as a disjunction and curly brackets as a conjunction of conditions, presented by equations and/or inequalities, is easy to grasp. However, finding the outcome solutionasacompositionofsolutionsofconstituentsrequiresexplicit studies. The capability of VisuMatica to display the ready solution of a system is an obligatory feature of math software and has a low educational effect. To enforce the activity of discovering the solution of a system, VisuMatica includes an option to graph solutions of all of its constituents. The task becomes more concentrated on the logical structure of the system: she looks for a proper region/s (ifany)asacompositionofthedisplayedones. The graphing method — the subject of our book — includes many specific approaches depending on these features. The possibility of receiving an immediate visual solution is a useful option. It can help but it cannot replace a strongly justified solution. 3.2 Inequalities The most popular method of solving inequalities is the method of intervals. Continuityisusuallynotindicatedherebutimplicitlymeant.This method is based on the Bolzano theorem, which states that if values of f(a) and f(b) of continuous function f have different signs, then the equation f(x)= 0 has at least one root on the interval (a,b). Thus, a function can change its sign only at its zero points or its points of discontinuity. In each interval between any two such sequential points, the function’s values remain positive/negative.

Functional Line in the Studies of Equations and Inequalities 185 We can consider the solution of bivariate inequalities f(x,y)◦0 as an extension of the univariate ones. The name changes properly and it becomes a method of regions or test point method instead of the method of intervals. All the ideas remain the same: (1) Solve and graph equation f(x,y) = 0 (2D curve(s) and/or points). (2) Substitute coordinates of some point from each region, bounded by these curves. (3) Define the solution as a union of proper regions, where the function’s value fits the inequality. In general, it is easy to show that (a + c,b + d) represents the vector defined by the diagonal of the parallelogram with vertices at (0, 0), (a,b), (c,d), and (a + c,b + d). Thus, the simple algebraic definition of addition for pairs leads to a simple geometric definition for adding planar vectors. Sometimes, two vectors are collinear and therefore do not form the sides of an “honest” parallelogram — in such a case, the parallelogram degenerates into four oriented segments belonging to a single line. As the formula (a,b) + (c,d) = (a + b,c + d) implies, the vector addition is commutative: u + v = v + u, and associative: (u+v)+w = u+(v+w). Use VisuMatica to model the addition of complex numbers and to visualize the basic properties of addition (see the file Complex numbers addition.grh). Hint: Utilize the condition/expression window. It is customary to let the letter i denote the vector (0, 1) and think of (1, 0) as being represented by the real number 1, also viewed as a vector. Thus, z = a(1,0) +b(0,1) = a1+bi, the later expression commonly abbreviated as a+bi. Note that the formulas above involve the multiplication of a vector by a scalar, which is not quite the same as the multiplication of vectors. If we want to be very formal, we should write (a,b) = (a,0) ∗(1,0) +(b,0) ∗(0,1) = (a,0)∗1+ (b,0)∗i, instead of (a,b) = a(1,0)+b(0,1). The polar form of 1 is {1,0} and of i is {1,π/2}. Therefore, i 2 = (0,1) 2 = {1,π/2}2 = {1,π} = (−1,0) = −1, which equals −1 in the universe of real numbers. Let us add and multiply complex numbers given in the form x1 + yi. The addition is easy: (a+bi)+(c+di) = (a+c)+(b+d)i. Multiplying is a little more complicated. Employing commutativity, distributivity, and associativity of the two operations, we get (a+bi)(c+di)= (a+bi)c+(a+bi)di = ac+bci+adi+bdi 2 = ac+bdi 2 +(ad+bc)i.

206 Mathematics Studies Through Technology: Precalculus, Calculus, and More Although we anticipate that every non-zero complex number z = {r,θ} has a reciprocal (a multiplicative inverse) 1/z = {1/r,−θ}, it is not obvious how to find it explicitly in the Cartesian form. Here is where the conjugation might help. First, note that (a+bi)(a−bi) = a2 +b2. Consider the quotient a+bi and multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjuc+di gate of c+di, i.e., by c−di: a+bi a+bi c−di (a+bi)(c−di) = ∗ =. c+di c+di c−di c2+d2 Hence, a+bi ac+bd ad−bc = −i. c+di c2+d2 c2+d2 Note that c2 +d2 is a real positive number. It represents the square of the length of the vector c + di. The length of the vector (c,d) is also called the absolute value or the modulus of the complex number c + di. √It is commonly denoted by |c + di| and is defined by the formula c2+d2. VisuMatica recognizes both |c + di| and mod(c+di) notations. Since the product of z = c + di and its conjugate z = c − di is c2 + d2, the absolute value of a complex number is equal to the squareroot of the product of the number and its conjugate:
|c+di| = (c+di)(c−di).
This has an important implication: the square of the distance d(z, w) between points z, w of the complex plane can be expressed in terms of arithmetic operations and conjugation. In fact, d(z,w) 2 = (z−w)(z −w). 210 Mathematics Studies Through Technology: Precalculus, Calculus, and More 4.8 Functions f: C → C: Equations and inequalities In the previous sections, we met examples of complex-valued functions with a complex argument. The universe of such functions is very rich and exciting. Suffice it to note that our good old real functions f:R → R of a real variable can beconsidered as a special case of similar functions with Domain and Range consisting of complex numbers with an imaginary part equal to zero. There is another familiar “parallel” universe of functions f: R 2 → R 2 that is similar to the new one. Indeed, if we recall the representation of complex numbers in the form of ordered pairs of real ones, we see the similarity of these worlds — they are both representable in the form f:(x,y) → (f 1(x,y),(f 2(x,y)). 2 properly). The understanding of the concept of limit, based on an intuitive definition, allows going further and in some way to “explain” the basic properties of limits by using graphs: rules for limits (limit of a

Limit and Continuity 225 sum equals to the sum of limits, etc.), the Squeeze theorem (if f(x) is sandwiched between two other functions, which have the same limit at a, then f(x) also has a limit at a, and it is the same), etc. One can create proper models, similar to the previous one and use them to explore and “prove” these features. These properties help solve exercises on finding a limit of numerous functions. It somehow “justifies” mathematics curricula of high schools, which is often limited by an intuitive interpretation of the concept. 2 Precise Definitions There are several strict definitions of the concept of functional limit. Textbooks on Calculus often consider two of them: the so-called definition by Cauchy (Augustin-Louis Cauchy (1789–1857)) and by Heine (Heinrich Eduard Heine (1821–1881)). 2.1 (ε,δ)-definition (Definition by Cauchy4) Theunderstandingof thecloseness ofx toa, expressedbyinequality x−a < δ withsmallenoughδ, was fruitfulinmodelingtheintuitive definition of the concept of limit. Actually, we were looking for two f(x): closenesses, related to function closeness of argument x to a correspondent f(x) to the value of and as a result, closeness of the limit L. Butitiswrongtoexpectthesameδ x−a < inbothinequalities: δ and |f(x)−L| < δ. We have prepared to realize this fact in Tasks 3, and 4 of Tasks 1.2. In some cases, we must push x extremely close to a to guarantee f(x)−L < δ. This argumentation in class is finalized by the introduction of the following ε−δ definition: L f(x) x → a D2 The number is called the limit of function as if and only if, for every ε > 0, there exists δ > 0 such that f(x)−L < ε, < x−a < δ. whenever 0 4Was first given byBernard Bolzano in 1817.

Not surprisingly, the formation of the concept of the limit based on this definition is traditionally very difficult. Clarification of definition using the following formal logical notation, which includes both universal and existence quantifiers and an implication, stresses even more: D3 The number L is called the limit of function f(x) as x → a if and only if (∀ε > 0)(∃δ > 0)(0 < |x−a|< δ ⇒ |f(x)−L|< ε). ◦ What is different in the behavior of the sequences?
◦ What does the difference mean?
Consideration of the uniquearrangement of random sequences on horizontal lines and its application to the solution can be interesting and informative: (1) Rewriting initial equality z = x/y in form x = yz explains the surface geometry. (a) It is a rotated saddle-shaped hyperbolic paraboloid. (b) The surface has a gap: it does not include points of the classical hyperbolic paraboloid with y = 0 (the denominator in the initial expression). From x = yz, we immediately conclude that all these points fill thez-axis (the darkened vertical line that from a proper point of view looks like a crack). (2) A hyperbolic paraboloid is a classical example of a ruled surface, i.e., throughevery pointofthissurfacepassesastraight linethat lies on it. (3) More specifically, our surface is a conoid because it fulfills the two following conditions: (a) All rulings (lines) are parallel to a plane, the directrix plane (z = 0). Thus, it is an example of a Catalan surface. (b) All rulings intersect a fixed line, the axis (z-axis). Our surface is a right conoid because its axis is perpendicular to its directrix plane. Therefore, all the rulings are perpendicular to the axis. (4) Setting z to a definite value, say, a, we get an equation of the contour line on level a and it is a =x/y or x = ay or y = x/a — a straight line — the directrix of our surface. Use the Linear element tab in the Geometry dialog box and define this line by two expressions: Point(x,x /a,a) and min min Point(x,x /a,a).Animateparameteraandmakesurethat max max this line does the directrix of the surface and at a certain point of time comprises all the points of a random sequence, predetermined by the direction angle. For each horizontal directrix, there is a direction angle atan(1/a) that also defines the proper

Domain and Range of both of them can be illustrated by a 2D plane.33 4.1 (ε,δ)-definition (Definition by Cauchy) We need some analogs to the concept of a neighborhood — the expression of closeness: We call a ε-neighborhood of a given point z o all points z lying inside a disk centered at z o with positive ε as radius, i.e.,
|z−z
o
| < ε.
We call punctured ε-neighborhood 0 < |z −z o | < ε all points in the ε-neighborhood of z o except for z o itself. We call point z o an accumulation point of a set S if each punctured neighborhood of z o contains at least one point of S. D11 We call L the limit of f(z) as z approaches an accumulation point z o (limz→z f(z) = L) if and only if for each positive 0 number ε, there is a positive number δ such that |f(z)−L|< ε, whenever 0 < |z−z o |< δ. All points of the plane that fit inequality |z − z p | < ρ form the interior of a circle centered at z p with radius ρ. Thus, the limz→z f(z) = L graphical interpretation is as follows: 0 For each circle of radius ε centered at w o, there exists a correspondent radius δ of a circle with center L that images of all its interior points (not necessarily including z o) that belong to Dom(f) lie inside the circle (L,ε). (2) Jump discontinuity: In this case, both one-sided limits exist and are finite but are not equal: lim f(x)= lim f(x). Thus, lim f(x) does not exist. x→a− x→a+ x→a The function f may have any value or not be defined at a. We call a a jump discontinuity or discontinuity of the first kind. The first Weierstrass theorem: The function f(x), continuous on a segment [a,b], is bounded on it, i.e., (∃m )(∃m )(∀x ∈ [a,b])m ≤ f(x)≤ m. 1 2 1 2

Sign:f(x)↓ (f(x)). Afunctionissaidtobeincreasing (weakly increasing) on an interval (a,b) if (f(x)≤ f(y)), (∀x,y ∈ (a,b))(x < y)⇒(f(x)< f(y)). Afunctionissaidtobedecreasing (weakly decreasing) onaninterval (a,b) if (f(x)≥ f(y)), (∀x,y ∈ (a,b))(x < y)⇒(f(x)> f(y)). A function, which is increasing/decreasing (weakly increasing/ 6 weakly decreasing), on the entire domain, is called monotonic. As a result of analyzing the fact that f 1(x) = 1 on each interval of continuity, we conclude that this is still not enough to sketch the graph. One should find the shortest way that provides enough information to solve the problem. After such materialized activities with the gradual removal of the hint, we are ready to move on to manual sketching. Computer-free graph sketching skills remain an important part of mathematical culture. In doing so, one can follow, for example, the steps outlined at the beginning of this section and perform some features of our model by hand. The practice of the choice of the minimum and sufficient set of these steps cultivates intuition and a deep understanding of the qualitative component of the formed knowledge: Figure 36.

So, completing our observations, we can say that if some function y = F(x) is an antiderivative of function f(x), then each function y = F(x) + c, with c ∈ R also an antiderivative of function f(x). Its graph can be obtained by shifting by c along the y-axis of the graph of function F(x) along the y-axis. It looks like the difference between any two antiderivatives of the same function is a constant function. Consider the following two examples of antiderivative (Zorich, 2015, p. 306): Example 1: The function F(x) = arctanx is a primitive of f(x) = 1 on the entire real line, since arctanx = 1. 1+x2 1+x2 Example 2: The function F(x) = arcctg 1 is a primitive of f(x) = x 1 on the set of positive real numbers and on the set of negative 1+x2 real numbers, since for x= 0 F (x) = − 1 · − 1 = 1 = f(x). 1+(1) 2 x2 1+x2 x

We started from y = 2sin(x) in M5.9 and got its derivative y = 2cos(x); now, we took the result of differentiation y = 2cos(x) and got its antiderivative: y = 2sin(x). It exhibits the mutuality of the operations of differentiation and indefinite integration. The considered question of finding an antiderivative, which graph passes through a certain point is an example of a general fundamental problem, the so-called Cauchy problem, about finding a solution to a differential equation for the given initial conditions. 2.2 Definite integral Since ancient times, people have been looking for ways to find the area of figures. This problem, which is important for applications, occupiedthemindsoftheancientGreeks, whoalreadyinthe5thcentury BC formulated the so-called “method of exhaustion”, according to which the area of a figure was considered as the limit of the areas of a sequence of inscribed polygons. Archimedes was able to find the area between the green segment of the parabola y = x2 and the interval [0,1], using this method (Fig. 45). He divided the segment into n small segments and found Figure 45.

372 Mathematics Studies Through Technology: Precalculus, Calculus, and More the sum of the areas of the corresponding rectangles. He took the limiting value of this sum at n →∝ as the value of the area. This idea, with various modifications, remains to this day. When calculating the area of a figure bounded by the graph of a function y = f(x) on the segment [a,b], the x-axis, and two vertical straight lines x = a and x = b (the so-called curvilinear trapezoid), one divides the segment by points a = x 0 < x 1 < x 2 <,...,< x n = b into partition P = [x 0,x 1),[x 1,x 2),..., [x n−1,x n]. On each of the intervals [x i,x i+1] formed in this way, a certain geometric figure is built: a rectangle, a trapezoid, a curved trapezoid bounded by a parabolathatapproximatesthesectionofthecurvey = f(x).Wecan calculate the area of such figures. The sum of these areas (positive, when the figure is located above the x-axis and negative otherwise) with an increase in the number of dividing points is taken as the “signed” area of the original curvilinear trapezoid. We call the norm of a partition the length of the longest subinterval max(x i −x i−1). For rectangles, D.2.2 the sum S = n i=1 f(x∗ i )(x i −x i−1) for function f and partition P, where x∗ is such an arbitrary number that i x i−1 ≤ x∗ i ≤ x i is called the Riemann sum. Depending on the x∗ position, are considered the following types of i Riemann sums: – Left Riemann sum, if x∗ i = x i−1 for all i∈ [1,n]. – Right Riemann sum, if x∗ i = x i for all i∈ [1,n]. – Middle Riemann sum, if x∗ i = (x i−1+x i)/2 for all i ∈ [1,n]. –Upper Riemann sum (upper Darboux sum), if S = n i=1 g i(x i −x i−1), where g i is the supremum of set f on the segment [x i−1,x i]. – Lower Riemann sum (lower Darboux sum), if S = n i=1 g i(x i −x i−1), where g i is the infimum of set f on the segment [x i−1,x i]. There are a few other ways to approximate the area of a curvilinear trapezoid that cannot be expressed in the form of Riemann sums:

• In the Simpson rule, instead of the side of a rectangle or trape-
zoid, the approximation uses a quadratic parabola that passes through points with coordinates M i−1(x i−1,f(x i−1)),M i∗((x i−1+ x i)/2,f((x i−1 +x i)/2)),M i(x i,f(x i)). This uses the Lagrange interpolation formula, which takes n points to define a polynomial of degree n − 1. Derivative and Integral 377 Let us list the classes of integrable functions:
• A function that is monotonic on a segment is integrable on it.
• Any function that is continuous in some segment is integrable on
this segment. Theclass of integrable functions also includes functions that are boundedon thesegment of integration and have afinitenumberof discontinuity points of the first kind (jump discontinuity) on this segment.
• If function f(x) is integrable on a segment [a,b], then the function
cf(x), where c is a constant, is integrable on this segment.
• If function f(x) is integrable on a segment [a,b], then the function
|f(x)| is also integrable on this segment.
• If functions f(x) and g(x) are integrable on the segment [a,b],
then their sum, difference, and product are also integrable on this segment.
• If function f(x) is integrable on a segment [a,b], then it is also
integrable on any part of this segment.
• If function f(x) is integrable on each part of a certain segment,
then it is integrable on the entire segment as well.
• If the values of a function to be integrated are changed in a finite
number of points by finite values, then the integrability of the function will not be violated. As applied to the function f(x), which is not defined at a finite number of points of the segment [a,b], this means that neither the existence of the integral nor its value depends on the values assigned to the function f(x) at the points of its discontinuity. bounded on this segment. This is a necessary condition of integrability. However, the inverse condition of the boundedness of the function is not sufficient for its integrability. Derivative and Integral 389 The integrand f 1(x) is continuous on [a,b]. According to the First Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, the function F(x) is an antiderivative of f 1(x). More precisely, this is the primitive that passes through the point (a,0). So, we have enough information to solve the problem. In fact, we are looking for the correct value of the constant c, associated with the antiderivative F(x), in the general formula y = f(x)dx + c = G(x) + c of indefinite integral, where G(x) is some primitive of f(x). This primitive in our case satisfies the condition0= G(a)+c.Therefore, c = −G(a).Hence, F(x) = G(x)−G(a). We got that b x f(x)dx = F(b) = G(b)−G(a), where F(x) = f(t)dt. a a The resulting conclusion is the outcome of the following: The Second Fundamental Theorem of Calculus: If function f is continuous on the segment [a,b] and F(x) is some of its primitives on this segment, then the Newton–Leibniz formula bf(x)dx = a F(b)−F(a) = F(x)|b is true. a This formula demonstrates the relationship between definite and indefinite integrals and provides a convenient mechanism for calcu-26 lating the value of a definite integral. # Chapter 6

Function as a Space Transformation∗ 1 Commercial Dynamic Geometry Software (DGS) provides a userfriendlyinterfacefortheconstructionof2Dand3Dgeometricobjects and their manipulation with them. Both activities implicitly or explicitly widely utilize affine transformations of these objects. Very often different objects (figures) are transformed differently in the same model. One can say with certainty that the smooth and gradual transformation of figures is the main mechanism and the main characteristic of these programs that ultimately led to their common name Dynamic.... Is the smooth and gradual figures’ transformation adequate to the mathematical notion of transformation? Not exactly. Transformationsarefunctions.Therefore, theyareone-stepactionsdefinedas correspondence. Thus, nobodythinksaboutthe graphof a quadratic function as a “result” of a smooth and gradual “deformation” of a straight line (x-axis) to the parabola form. Opposite, a line in the domain becomes a parabola in range in a one-step transformation. The only correct meaning of DGS as a dynamical system is the possibility to manually change and deform the studied model. ∗Transformation algebra and related issues of space transformation groups are far from the main line of thebook and are not discussed in it. 1CabriR II Plus, CabriR 3D, The Geometer’s SketchpadR, Cinderella, etc. 393

394 Mathematics Studies Through Technology: Precalculus, Calculus, and More As a rule, transformations are not processes (series of actions). They are processes and their actions are “changeable” in time in 2 specific cases, e.g., in the case of dynamical systems. 1 Linear Transformations Linear transformations are an obvious notion, studied in linear algebra and geometry. 1.1 Vector space Generally, linear transformations deal with linear spaces. D.1.1 Vector space (linear space) is a set V of elements called vectors, forwhichtheoperationsofadditionwitheach other 3 andmultiplicationbyanumber, ascalar, aredefined. These operations are subject to eight axioms: (1) (∀x,y ∈ V)x+y = y+x — commutativity of addition; (2) (∀x,y,z ∈V)x+(y+z)= (x+y)+z — associativity of addition; (3) (∃0∈ V)(∀x ∈ V)x+0 = 0+x = x — the existence of an identity element of addition (the zero vector); (4) (∃x ∈ V)(∀−x ∈ V)x+(−x) = 0 — the existence of an inverse element of addition; (5) (∀x ∈ V)(∀α,β)α(βx) = (αβ)x — associativity of multiplication by a scalar; (6) (∃x ∈ V)1·x = x—theexistenceofanidentity element of multiplication by a scalar; (7) (∀x ∈ V)(∀α,β)(α+β)x = αx+βx — distributivity of scalar multiplication over scalar addition; (8) (∀x,y ∈ V)(∀α)α(x+y)= αx+αy — distributivity of scalar multiplication over vector addition. 2VisuMatica provides dynamic processing, but the geometry subjects do not limit it. It supports deep studies of different mathematical courses and subjects, in particular, discussed here. 3Weconsider herescalars as real numbers.

Function as a Space Transformation 395 Examples: (1) The set C of complex numbers with standard operations of complex numbers’ addition and multiplication by a real number. (2) The sets of m×n matrices with standard operations of matrix addition and multiplication by a real number. (3) Considering geometric points as vectors with the corresponding coordinates P(x 1,x 2,...,x n), the result of the operation of points’ addition — as a point with sums of correspondent coordinates of the summands, specifically P 1(x 11,x 12,...,x 1n)+ P 2(x 21,x 22,...,x 2n) = P 3(x 11 + x 21,x 12 + x 22,...,x 1n + x 2n), and the product of a point P(x 1,x 2,...,x n) by a scalar α as a point P (αx 1,αx 2,...,αx n), we obtain another example of a linear space R n = {(x 1,x 2,...,x n)|x 1,x 2,...,x n ∈R}. This finite-dimensional vector space supports the operation of scalar vector product: a function f:(v 1,v 2) → r ∈ R by the following rule: (v 1,v 2) =((x 11,x 12,...,x 1n),(x 21,x 22,...,x 2n)) =x 11 x 21+x 12 x 22+···+x 1n x 2n. This Euclidean space allows us to determine its metric characteristics: length |v| of vector v as (v,v), the distance between two vectors v 1 and v 2 as |v 1 − v 2 |, and the angle (v,v ) between them as 1 2.

Function as a Space Transformation 403 So, the linear transformation of a two-dimensional plane and three-dimensional space does not simply (generally speaking) change the position of all points. It does this in such a way that results in the following: • The images of lines passing through any two points are lines pass-
|  | ing through |  | the images | of | these points. |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
• The images of the line segments connecting any two points are the
|  | segments | connecting |  | the | images of these points. |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
• The ratios of the lengths of segments, that lie on the same or
parallel straight lines, remain the same for the images of these segments.
• Images of parallel lines are parallel.
Remark: For horizontal and vertical lines, visual confirmation of parallelism is easily demonstrated when the mapping style is set to a grid (see blue arrows in Fig. 6). Thus, to build an image of an arbitrary polygon or polyhedron, it is sufficient to find the images of its vertices and connect them in the same order as in the original figure. This fact is actively used in computer graphics, where planar and spatial figures are often presented as a result of triangulation: in the formofaunionoftriangles—thesimplestpolygons. Theiranimation is often nothing more than a series of linear transformations. So, we have built the image of the polygon. How about images of its internal points? Knowledge of the properties of linear transformations will help us here too. Let us find out the answer using the example of the mechanism for painting the image of the left view (the colored rectangle — the visibleareaofthedomainoftransformationasafunction)intheright view (the parallelogram of the set of images of the points’ values of the function). The gray line connecting the point pointed by the mouse with its image serves as a convenient tool for clarifying the fundamental concept of an eigenvector. Aneigenvector ofalineartransformationisanon-zerovector, the image of which is a collinear vector — the same vector multiplied by some scalar value (it can be equal to 0). The scalar by which the eigenvector is multiplied is called the eigenvalue of the linear transformation corresponding to the given eigenvector. Formally, ofalineartransformationf:V → V D.1.5 aneigenvector ofvector space V is such a vector x= 0 that f(x)= λx. λ The number is called the eigenvalue of the linear transformation f:V → V of vector space V if there exists such x= f(x)= λx. eigenvector 0 that

Thus, by definition, the eigenvector and its image lie on the same straight line that passes through the origin. Moreover, if the scalar-eigenvalue λ > λ < 0, then the vectors are directed in one direction, and if 0, then in the opposite directions. Inconcludingthissection, weneedadditionalconceptsthatwillallow us to clarify and take a fresh look at linear transformations of space. 1.3 Dimension and basis of a vector space D.1.9 The dimension of a vector space is the maximum number of linearly independent vectors in this space. D.1.10 The basis of a vector space is an ordered set of linearly independent vectors of this space, the number of which is equal to the dimension of the space. In the space of n-dimensional vectors, consider n unit vectors of the form e 1 = (1,0,...,0) e 2 = (0,1,...,0).... e n = (0,0,...,1) This system of vectors is linearly independent, and no vector can be added to this system withoutviolating its linear independence. Since the number of vectors in it is equal to n, then the dimension of the space of n-dimensional vectors is equal to n, and the unit vectors e 1,e 2,...,e n are the basis of this space. Rearranging the vectors of the system e 1,e 2,...,e n, we obtain other bases.

Function as a Space Transformation 423 If we take a linearly independentsystem of non-unitvectors, then n-dimensional it is also the basis of an vector space. The basis of a two-dimensional vector space area any two noncollinearvectors. Thebasisofathree-dimensionalspaceareanythree non-coplanar vectors. Theorem: Any vector of an n-dimensional vector space is uniquely decomposed in terms of a basis. e,e,...,e n-dimensional Let 1 2 n be the basis of an vector space. Let us add an n-dimensional vector x to these vectors. Then, the resulting system of vectors will be linearly dependent and the vector x can be uniquely linearly expressed in terms of the vectors e,e,...,e 1 2 n: x = x e 1+x e 2+···+x e n, where x,x,...,x — scalars. 1 2 n 1 2 n D.1.11 The coefficients x 1,x 2,...,x n are called the coordinates of e,e,...,e the vector x in the basis 1 2 n. x The same vector in a different basis will have different coordinates. 426 Mathematics Studies Through Technology: Precalculus, Calculus, and More However, these observations have clarified the meaning of the elements of the transformation matrix, which until now seemed to be arbitrary numbers. The columns of the transformation matrix are the coordinates of the images of the basis vectors. These coordinates completely define the linear transformation. This fact extends in an obvious way to linear transformations of spaces of any dimension n. | 2 Nonlinear | Space | Transformations | (NLST) |
In “the ‘real’ world problems and issues on the frontiers of modern scientific, technological, economic, and social research are often nonlinear. In this nonlinear world, many of the mathematical concepts andtools learned andappliedintraditional undergraduate, andeven
| graduate, science | coursesaresimplyinadequate, andnewmathemat- |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ical tools | must be introduced” | (Enns, 2010, | p. XI). |
In general, the demarcation line between the world of linear and nonlinear phenomena is based on the following fact: at the same increment of the independentvariable, anonlinear function responds differently depending on the variable value, while the linear function responds identically. A fundamental property of nonlinear functions is the almost complete indifference to changes in some values of the independent variables and increased sensitivity to changes in other
| values of | the independent | variables. |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

Function as a Space Transformation 447 Nonlinearphenomenaaredescribedbynonlinearmappingsordifferential equations. Informally, weclassify nonlinear spatialtransformations supported by VisuMatica by the • space S dimension (1D, 2D, 3D); • underlying computational domain (R, C); • transforming action (One Step, Continuous, Discrete). Table 1 illustrates this arrangement with some examples (in black) and suitable notions. Visualization of spatial transformation is radically different from visualization of figure transformation. In the case of the transformation of a figure, both the figure and its image are located in the same domain and can be shown and explored there, while space transformation “changes” the entire space and therefore assumes simultaneous presentation of both spaces — Domain and Range. As a result, theregular Cartesianway becomesunusableinthecaseof morethan one-dimensional domain. 21 VisuMatica solves this problem by presenting the Domain and Range in two separate “synchronized” views. Table 1. 21Cartesiancoordinatesystemallowsshowingf:R→Rfunctionsbyduplicating spacedimensions:x-axispresentsthefunction’sDomainandy-axisitsRange.In this manner, for visualizing 2D or 3D space transformation, one needs2×2=4 or 3×2=6 dimensions.

448 Mathematics Studies Through Technology: Precalculus, Calculus, and More
| What | are the mental |  | activities | while studying | NLST | that the |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
software has to help interiorize? Mainly, they are the same as in the case of any other transformations: NLST, being functions, require
| consolidation | of the | following | two | complementary | actions: |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| • finding | the image | of an | element | or a subset | of the Domain, |  |
• finding the preimage of an element or a subset of the Range.
Although these activities are the most important and their assimilation includes inter alia mastering mapping, fixed point, root-finding, etc., educational software has to support a deeper and wider exploration of NLST features and behavior. The following case studies present VisuMatica’s support of these pedagogical tasks. We selected these simpleand popularexamples to emphasize the strength of educational software as a tool for a deep and wide exploration of the studied subject that allows discovering newandsurprisingfeatures “everywhere”, even ina“boring”and/or well-known math. 2.1 One-step NLST 2.1.1 1D mapping In this simplest and easiest case, it seems that nothing special should be done in addition to regular math studies at secondary and high school. We have studied graphs of linear and nonlinear, e.g., quadratic, functions and made a lot of exercises of finding function f(a) f(x) b. values and roots of equations = The mentioned activities of finding images and preimages of transformation are already consolidated. We are familiar with the term linear and notions of linear function, andlineardependence andmanagethemacceptably. Their dimension was the sum of the dimensions (the number of independent real variables) of the domain and the range of corresponding functions. Indeed, given that the model of a real number is the number line (1D), a function y = f(x) is represented mainly by curves on the plane (f:R → R,1D + 1D = 2D), and a function z = f(x,y) by (f:R2 → R,2D+1D 3D). surfaces in 3D space = Quiteunexpectedly, even in the seemingly simple quadratic equations is hidden a multidimensional 4D (!) nature, the study of which can reveal new colors of even such a rather boring concept. 23 2.1.2.2 A new look at quadratic equations We are going to demonstrate that exploration of the mapping between alternate two-parameter representations can enliven the study of quadratic polynomials. Remarkably, through this approach, all monic 24 quadratic equations x2 +bx+c = 0 with real roots can be solved at once and all their solutions are presented in a single display! 2.1.2.4 The discriminant curve and tangents The parabolic boundary that discriminates between the image and non-image points under the root-to-coefficient map V is called the discriminant curve. Moving the mouse pointer in the coefficient plane and observing its preimages, bluecircles in theroot plane, we come to the following conclusions: This discriminant curve is the image of the diagonal line {r 1 = r 2 }, that is, the family of quadratic equations with equal roots(or, moreappropriately, withasinglerootofmultiplicity 2). It turns out that the image of this diagonal line is a parabola. Moreover, the points on or below this parabola are the V-images of points from the root-space, and the points above the parabola have no preimages. If this is the case, then the discriminant parabola is indeed a “discriminating” curve. To test this assumption, let us add a graph of the diagonal line, of the function r 2 = r 1 to our model. We were right; our discriminant curve is its image (Fig. 42). It is relatively easy to find the equation of the image of {r 1 = r 2 } under the Viete map V. Points on this diagonal line are of the form (r,r). Under the map V: (r 1,r 2) → (b,c), a typical point (r,r) maps to the point (−2r,r2 ). Therefore, b(r) = −2r, and c(r) = r2. The representation {b(r) = −2r,c(r) = r2} describes this parabola parametrically. Solving the first equation for r and substituting the

It is somewhat surprising to realize the following: Observed at a large scale (which magnifies b and c evenly),almost all quadratic equations with real coefficients have real roots! 2.1.2.6 Changing dimension Let us develop a new, three-dimensional view of the space of monic quadratic equations x2 + bx + c = 0. Think of such an equation as a relation imposed on the three quantities: x,b, and c. The triple (b,c,x)canberegardedasapointofthethree-dimensionalCartesian space R 3. Then, the relation x2 +bx+c = 0 defines a surface S in 3 R — the quadratic equation surface. We can rewrite the equation of this surfacein the form c = −x2− bx =−x(x+b). This form suggests that S is a graph of the function g(x,b) = −x(x+b) over the xb-plane in R 3. This function takes the value zero along the pair of intersecting lines x = 0 and x+b = 0 in the xb-plane. It is positive only in the sector {x > 0,x+b > 0} and in the sector {x < 0,x+b < 0}. The graph c= g(x,b) is a quadratic surface shaped like a saddle (see Fig. 59; file Quadratic Equation Surface.grh) — it is a hyperbolic paraboloid we are familiar from the section on quadrics in Chapter 3. Now, let us take a different look at the surface S, from the vantage point of the coefficient bc-plane. Imagine that we are located at a point (b,c,0) in the space and are looking in a direction perpendicular to the bc-plane. Where will our ray of sight pierce the surface? Clearly, at a point of the form (b,c,x), which belongs to the surface {x2 + bx + c = 0}. In other words, the perpendicular to the coefficient plane through the point (b,c,0) will hit S at points (b,c,r), where r is the root of equation x2 +bx+c = 0. Recall that such a quadratic equation has real solutions only if (b,c) is located below or on the discriminant parabola. Thus, when (b,c) is in the region {c < b2/4}, thentheperpendicularwillintersectthesurfaceS attwo pointswhosex-coordinatesarethetworealrootsoftheequation. For points (b,c) on the discriminant parabola, the intersection consists of a single point whose x-coordinate is the only real root −b/2 (of multiplicity two). Finally, if (b,c) is in the region {c > b2/4}, then the intersection is empty.

Other examples of 2D to 2D mappings are functions of a complex variable, and we turn to the consideration of possibilities of their studying using the software. 2.1.3 2D mapping: Complex plane The studyof functions of complex variables deals mainly with NLST f:C → C. All the elements of VisuMatica’s mapping resources are applicable in the complex case. 2.1.3.1 Linear transformation Let us start to study the complex Domain by creating a very simple tool for checking linearity by analogy with the f:R 2 → R 2 case. There are at least three options to construct such a tool. At the very beginning, we start creating a new model with a definition of two complex numbers c 1 and c 2, say, c 1:= a + b ∗ i, c 2:= c+d∗i, and the function as w = c 1 ∗z+c 2. The First way: Add a segment arrow to our model in the same manner as in the V-mapping case, and the tool is ready (see the file w = c 1 ·z +c 2 Linearity.grh). It includes two freely movable points P and Q and a segment arrow that begins at P and ends at P +Q. Dragging the P point with the mouse brings up an opposite result to the one shown in Fig. 47: the image of the segment arrow remains a segment arrow. After any change of parameters a,b,c, or d, the dragging also does not change the direction and length of the image. Select and move point Q. The original vector changes as well as its image. Unselect the point Q and repeat the experiment by dragging point P. Our transformation of complex plane w = c 1 ∗ z + c 2 is linear.
