Usethemodelin thefileInversion transformation-Any center.grh to check your solution. Riemann sphere: Bernhard Riemann proposed a new geometric interpretation of the set of complex numbers. He placed them on a sphere, called the Riemann sphere. To show how each complex number is associated with a point on the sphere position, the sphere with the “south pole” at the origin of the complex plane and from the “north pole” draws rays to each 39The intersection points belong to the inversion circle, about which we know that its points coincide with their images.

496 Mathematics Studies Through Technology: Precalculus, Calculus, and More point of the plane. The point at which the ray going to the number z z intersects the sphere is called the point on the Riemann sphere. At the same time, one point of the sphere, namely, the “north pole”, does not correspond to any complex number. However, if we make thenumber“move” along the complex planeto infinity (in any direction), then its image on the Riemann sphere will approach the “north pole”. This allowed Riemann to call the “north pole” the point of infinity and to add it to the complex plane, thus obtaining an extended complex plane C = C∪∞. The concepts of the real and imaginary parts of the point ∞ are not defined. Arithmetic operations of complex numbersare extended by defining, for any z ∈C, z +∞ = ∞,z ·∞ = ∞ for any z= 0, ∞/0 ∞ 0/∞ ∞·∞ ∞. ∞+∞,∞−∞, = and = 0, and = Herewith, and 0·∞ are undefined. 40 The images in Figs. 80(a) and 80(b)) show the mapping of a large blue point on the plane, corresponding to the position of the mouse pointer in the domain view, onto the sphere of radius 0.5. If an opaque sphere does not cover this point, then the visible part is depicted as a solid, bold red segment, and the remaining, hidden part, as a thin dashed red line that connects the blue point of the plane with the north pole of the sphere. Theprojection ontothesphere(thepointwheretherayintersects with it) is shown as a bold red dot if it is visible and a small red dot if it is invisible. The equator of the sphere is drawn in orange. The red arrows in Figs. 80(c) and 80(d) present the Mapping 2D settings that allow this to show as an empty mapping style onto an opaque sphere with the domain plane touching the sphere at the south. It has a lot of interesting features. We consider just a few of them here. c M(z) az b When = 0, we have = d + d, i.e., a familiar linear transformation of the complex plane that can beexpressed as a coma a position of rotation by the angle of arg( ), scaling by mod( ), and d d b translation by. d

510 Mathematics Studies Through Technology: Precalculus, Calculus, and More In the case of c= 0, we have the following expression: 43 az+b bc−ad 1 a M(z) = = · +. cz+d c2 z+ d c c Thus, M(z) can be presented as the following sequence of plane transformations: Here, t 1(z) and t 4(z) are translation transformations, t 2(z) is a reciprocal transformation, and t 3(z) is a composition of rotation and scaling transformations. Every M¨obius transformation can be performed in the following three steps: (1) projection of the complex plane onto a sphere, (2) rigid motion of the sphere, (3) projection back from the sphere onto the plane. In particular, this motion of the sphere is a composition of the following transformations:
• Translation: M(z) = z+b, when a = 1, c = 0, d = 1.
• Dilation (scaling):M(z) = az, whena ∈Randb = 0,c = 0,d = 1.
• Rotation: M(z) = az, when |a| = 1 and b = 0, c= 0, d = 1.
• Reciprocal transformation: M(z) = 1, when a = 1, b = 0, c = 1,

Inthecaseofmultivaluedanalytic functionsofasingle complex variable, the proposed solution is called The Riemann Surface. On a technical level, the construction of Riemann surfaces is based on the principle of analytic continuation. However, here we adopt a more geometrical viewpoint. At first glance, the idea of a Riemann surface looks like a cheap trick: we replace the domain of a given multivalued function with a new more complex domain on which the function becomes singlevalued. Let us illustrate this trick with t√he simplest possible example. Take the two-valued function w = z of the complex variable z. 2 Consider the complex algebraic curve (the real surface) Σ in C {w2 z}, w u+ whose equation is = a complex parabola. If = iv and z = x+ iy, then, in the real uvxy-space, Σ can also be described {x u2−v 2,y 2uv}. by two quadratic polynomial equations: = √ = As we try to express w in terms of z, we get w = z, our original two-valued function. √ C, z, Now√, replace the domain of with the curve/surface Σ and f(z) = z with the coordinate w, viewed as a single-valued function w 2 on Σ. (The coordinate is a map from C to C and can be applied to any subset in its domain, including the complex curve Σ.) This z → complex curve Σ, equipped with the coordinate map√s: Σ C and

Function as a Space Transformation 537 vector fields supporting mechanism in our exploration. The notion of a vector field is crucial for describing differential equations and dynamical systems. Vectors there are interpreted as velocity. Mainly, only their slope is taken into account while the magnitude is ignored or scaled to suit the visualization needs. So, considering this circumstance, the interface must be explicitly configured on proper vectors’ portray. (Figure 119 shows an interpretation of the 2D and 3D nonlinear mapping using vector fields.) The following section presents the capabilities of VisuMatica in studies of continuous-time dynamical systems. Considering differential equations as continuous-time dynamical systems, the answer must be NOT. The cognitive value of visualization directly depends on its potential for exploration of the studied subject. Keeping in mind that the task of the theory of ordinary differential equations is to reconstruct the past and predict the future of the process, we conclude that the trajectories’ view in Fig. 123 does not provide such information. A known way of fixing this problem (still not sufficient) lies in showing trajectories together with direction arrows along them. VisuMatica offers a different, more informative approach to displaying trajectories as colored with a special color-coding pattern.

Detailed examination of ODE solutions with intensive use of the mentioned notions allows for conceiving a wide depiction of their behavior. 2.2.2 Global Exploration We have already seen some options for a global exploration of dynamical systems as an artifact in VisuMatica’s drawing mechanism (Fig. 125). At the same time, VisuMatica includes some special aids for this purpose. The aim here is to visualize the nature of the continuously processed transformation of a dynamical system that acts overall on the phase space and transforms it into itself. Specific studies of stability by the definition require additions to the mentioned visualization means. VisuMatica includes the ability to show a tube of some radius around any orbit. This allows modeling the neighborhood of the orbit, referred to in the definition. This tube is produced by a circle (3D) or segment (2D) with a center on the orbit, which we are checking on stability. Circle/segment slides along the trajectory keeping a “normal” orientation. More specifically,
• In the general case of 2D/3D phase space, it is a segment/circle,
which is perpendicular to the tangent of the trajectory. • It is perpendicular to the time axis if the phase space includes the t-axis. Thus, in the case of the first-order equation x˙ = f(x), x-axis

Like a sculpture, we observe the orbit from different points of view (instead of movingaround the sculpture, werotate the3Dvolume withthehelp of the software interface). 582 Mathematics Studies Through Technology: Precalculus, Calculus, and More of circle definition that are suitable for this goal: a circle, whose plane is normal to the orbit that passes through its center, and a circle, which is defined by a center and a normal vector to its plane (Fig. 156). The problem of precision arises when one tries to redefine the plane manually. To solve it, VisuMatica automatically reduces the precision of calculations to prevent the screen’s “freezing” and restores settings, when we release the mouse button. At first sight, something similar to the first image in Fig. 156 is displayed in Fig. 157, which depicts the orbit of the Lorenz attractor (see the file Lorenz attractor with Poincare mapping.grh): the single spiral just becomes a dual one. The balls’ points of intersection are also similarly located close one to another. But the difference is much more serious, and it is easily recognizable in the non-regular distribution of the ball’s colors in the Lorenz attractor. Increasing the precision of the calculation does not lead to the effect of orbit shrinkage we have seen in the case of a periodic cycle. The strange behavior of the Lorenz attractor manifested in the fact that it never repeats and chaotically proceeds: two close points on the attractor become randomly far away from each other later. Let us slightly perturb the initial point of the orbit: instead of coordinates (1.0, 0.01, 0.48) — left column in Fig. 158 — assign a new triplet: (1.00000001, 0.01, 0.48) — the right column. The perturbation is tiny: we’ve added 0.00000001 to the x-coordinate. 92 We received a surprisingly different result. Everything has changed: orbit, intersection points, and distribution of colors. The lower row in Fig. 158 shows exclusively the intersection points — the Poincar´e mapping, which is coded geometrically as the location of points supplemented with visually colored coding of their sequence. The geometry here is rather similar, but the color difference tells the true story about chaotic behavior: these two orbits at the same time t are very far from each other. Figure 159 shows two ways of confirmation of the noticed difference:

3 Conclusions This book demonstrates a new way of software support for teaching and learning mathematics. Unlike applets and specific models in CAS and DG systems, here creation and tuning mechanisms have a generic nature. This approach allows for emphasizingandexploiting themultidisciplinary and interdisciplinary links, the unity of mathematics, and thus eases the study of different mathematical subjects. The following distinguishing features of VisuMatica • absence of special syntax for definition and configuration of mathematical objects, • intensive use of the powerful potential of the user interface,
• attainment of dynamicity by manual manipulations with mouse
and sliders, • information visualization by colored coding help explore complicated mathematical notions and get an insight into their properties and relationships. Analysis of the visual artifacts pays attention to the limitations of the software and hardware processing and fosters criticality in evaluating the computing results.

Supplementary Material The supplementary material includes the following: a special version of the software VisuMatica; a short user guide; files with all the models, mentioned in this book; all the book’s figures in true colors.
